content: This condition is often attributed to reduced aortic compliance, which tends to occur with advancing age. Treatment of Systolic Hypertension Numerous randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have demonstrated the benefits of treating systolic hypertension. Below are detailed findings from key studies: SHEP Study The Systolic Hypertension in the Elderly Program (SHEP) trial demonstrated a reduction of three strokes per 100 patients treated over a five-year period. Patient Criteria: Participants had an SBP between 160 and 219 mmHg and a DBP below 90 mmHg. Patients with a history of stroke resulting in residual paresis or other neurological disabilities were excluded. Treatment Goal: The target was either a 20 mmHg reduction in SBP or achieving an SBP below 160 mmHg, whichever was lower. Outcomes: Syst-Eur Trial The Systolic Hypertension in Europe (Syst-Eur) trial showed a reduction of 0.3 strokes per 100 patients treated over a median follow-up of two years. Patient Criteria: Participants had an SBP between 160 and 219 mmHg and a DBP below 95 mmHg. Treatment Goal: The aim was to reduce sitting SBP by at least 20 mmHg or to achieve an SBP below 150 mmHg. Outcomes: HYVET Trial The Hypertension in the Very Elderly Trial (HYVET) included a subgroup analysis of patients aged 80 years or older, who predominantly had systolic hypertension. Patient Criteria: Treatment Goal: Outcomes: Patient Criteria: Participants were 75 years or older with hypertension but without diabetes. Exclusion criteria included a history of stroke or an SBP below 110 mmHg after one minute of standing. Treatment Goal: The study compared an intensive treatment target of SBP below 120 mmHg with a standard treatment target of SBP below 140 mmHg. Outcomes: Treatment Goals and Safety Considerations Based on these studies, targeting an SBP of 140 mmHg appears safe, provided the DBP remains at or above 68 mmHg. A re-analysis of SHEP data suggests that allowing DBP to drop below 70 mmHg may increase the risk of adverse effects. A meta-analysis of individual patient data from RCTs identified a nadir DBP of 85 mmHg, below which cardiovascular outcomes worsened in both untreated and treated hypertensive patients. However, interpreting these findings is challenging. Avoiding a DBP below 68-70 mmHg seems prudent, as: The nadir DBP of 85 mmHg in the meta-analysis is higher than the 68-70 mmHg nadir suggested by major RCTs on isolated systolic hypertension. The largest trials in the meta-analysis (HDFP and MRC1) primarily included middle-aged patients with diastolic hypertension before treatment. The independent effects of comorbid conditions versus treatment-related effects remain unclear. More recent analyses, including data from the SPRINT trial, have yielded conflicting results: Others recommend avoiding DBP below 70 mmHg. In patients with tight diabetic control, no clear relationship was observed. Practice Guidelines The 2018 European Society of Cardiology/European Society of Hypertension (ESC/ESH) guidelines recommend: For patients with coronary artery disease, targeting a DBP below 80 mmHg but not less than 70 mmHg. The 2017 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) guidelines do not specifically address low DBP.
